claims.text: SPD followed by short-duration, low-temperature sub-recrystallization annealing will produce a hierarchical microstructure in MPEAs.
The resulting hierarchical microstructure will contain high-density dislocation tangles and nanoscale precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates will act as both dislocation sources and dislocation barriers.
The proposed treatment will break the strength-ductility trade-off in MPEAs.
The candidate initial state is a coarse-grained, single-phase FCC or BCC MPEA with low dislocation density.
The initial alloy's room-temperature brittleness arises from limited slip-system activation or grain-boundary embrittlement.
Room-temperature HPT or ECAP will reduce grain size into the submicron or nanometer regime.
Annealing at 0.3-0.4 Tm for 10-30 minutes will remain below the recrystallization threshold.
The treated material will contain an ultra-high dislocation density of approximately 10^15 m^-2 within nanograins.
Short annealing will form coherent nanoscale solute-rich clusters or precipitates that pin dislocations without initiating cracks.
The treatment will increase the fraction of low-energy grain boundaries.
SPD introduces geometrically necessary dislocations and grain boundaries that raise yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening described as the Hall-Petch effect.
Short annealing permits nanoscale precipitation and internal-stress relaxation without significant grain growth.
Grain-boundary dislocation generation will enable uniform plastic deformation in a dislocation-starvation regime.
Precipitates and refined grains will retain high strength while grain-boundary dislocation sources improve ductility.
The treated alloy will show a yield-strength increase greater than 30% relative to the initial state.
The treated alloy will show a uniform-elongation increase greater than 15% relative to the initial state.
The treated alloy will have significantly greater total energy absorption than both the initial brittle state and standard annealed states.

Standard solution annealing followed by slow cooling typically produces coarse grains and low dislocation density, leading either to high ductility with low strength or to precipitation-strengthened material with low ductility.
Coarse precipitates produced during conventional precipitation hardening cause low ductility through premature void nucleation.

contradictions.description: The proposed structure is said to retain an ultra-high density of about 10^15 m^-2 dislocations within nanograins, while the mechanism is described as a 'dislocation starvation' regime. These descriptions are in tension unless starvation is explicitly defined as a dynamic depletion-and-replenishment process.

The outcome claims superiority over standard annealed states, but the experiment includes initial, SPD-only, and SPD-plus-annealed samples without a standard solution-annealed and slow-cooled comparison group.
